items.title: Feasibility and safety of a 6-month outpatient rehabilitation program combining therapeutic electrical stimulation using belt electrodes and nutritional management in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a pilot study.
items.abstract: Although resistance training with nutritional intervention is recommended for sarcopenia, effective programs are often difficult to implement in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility and safety of a 6-month outpatient rehabilitation program combining therapeutic electrical stimulation (TES) using belt electrodes with nutritional management in patients with RA. This pilot study was conducted as a prospective observational study with a single-arm before-after framework and enrolled outpatients with RA in remission or with low disease activity. Participants received an outpatient rehabilitation program as part of routine clinical practice once or twice weekly over 6 months, including TES applied to the lower limbs using belt electrodes (20 min per session; 20 Hz; maximum tolerable intensity) and the daily intake of an L-leucine-enriched protein-containing nutritional supplement. Feasibility and safety were evaluated based on study completion, TES session frequency, verbally confirmed adherence to nutritional supplementation, adverse events documented during the program, and maintenance of disease activity. Lower-limb lean mass, knee extensor muscle strength, and gait speed were assessed as exploratory clinical outcomes at baseline and after 6 months. Of the 14 recruited outpatients with RA, 10 completed both the 6-month program and the final outcome assessment, corresponding to a study completion rate of 71.4%. Participants received a median of 34.5 TES sessions over 6 months. As exploratory clinical outcomes, the median paired changes in lower-limb lean mass, knee extensor muscle strength, and gait speed were 0.08 kg (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.00 to 0.25; P  = 0.043), 1.58 kgf (95% CI, -0.35 to 7.25; P  = 0.084), and 0.18 m/s (95% CI, -0.04 to 0.24; P  = 0.084), respectively. Disease activity remained within the low disease activity to remission range and did not significantly change during the 6-month observation period ( P  = 0.214). No joint-related or cardiovascular adverse events were documented. This pilot study provides preliminary information on the feasibility and safety of a 6-month outpatient rehabilitation program combining TES using belt electrodes and nutritional management in patients with RA. These findings may inform the design of future studies.

items.title: Association of phenotypic and functional characteristics of regulatory T cells from minor salivary glands with expression of the delta 7 FoxP3 splice variant in patients with Sjögren's disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of exocrine glands, including minor salivary glands (MSG), with potential formation of ectopic germinal centers. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are critical suppressors of autoimmune responses, and their dysfunction has been implicated in SjD pathogenesis. FoxP3, the master transcription factor of Tregs, undergoes alternative splicing to produce four variants: full-length (FL), Δ2, Δ7, and Δ2Δ7. While FoxP3 splice variants are known to influence Treg proliferation and suppressive activity, their profile and functional significance in Tregs from SjD patients remain poorly characterized. Peripheral blood was collected from 20 SjD patients or 20 healthy donors (HD). MSG biopsies were obtained from 10 SjD patients. Tregs were isolated from blood and biopsy tissue by immunomagnetic separation and expanded ex vivo. FoxP3 splice variant mRNA levels were quantified by real-time RT-PCR. Treg phenotype (CD4, CD25, CD127, CD152, Helios), suppressive molecules (CD39, CD223, granzymes A/B, perforin), was assessed by flow cytometry. The concentrations of suppressive cytokines IL-10 andIL-35 were accessed by Bio-Plex assay. Proliferation was evaluated by cell counting. Suppressive activity was determined by mixed lymphocyte reaction. Splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) were used to induce Δ7 FoxP3 expression to confirm direct functional effects. Peripheral blood Tregs from SjD patients showed significantly decreased increased Δ7 FoxP3 splice variant compared to HD. MSG-derived Tregs from SjD patients also predominantly expressed the Δ7 FoxP3 variant. High-expressing Δ7 FoxP3 Tregs exhibited reduced proliferative activity, division frequency and decreased suppressive activity compared to low-expressing Δ7 FoxP3 Tregs. High-expressing Δ7 FoxP3 Tregs showed significantly reduced CD127low and Helios expression, decreased CD39, CD223, granzyme, and granzyme B. IL-10 and IL-35 production was also reduced. SSO-mediated induction of Δ7 FoxP3 MSG-derived Tregs confirmed these phenotypic and functional changes. This study demonstrates that elevated Δ7 FoxP3 splice variant expression in MSG-derived Tregs from SjD patients is associated with impaired proliferative and suppressive function, reduced expression of suppressive molecules and cytokines, and a phenotype suggestive of a transitional or immature Treg state. The results highlight the functional consequences of altered FoxP3 alternative splicing in SjD pathogenesis and suggest a possible involvement of Tregs in the biology of ectopic germinal centers in SjD.

items.title: Preferential phosphodiesterase inhibition as a novel strategy to modulate key pathways in systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease marked by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. The high disease burden and impact on quality of life highlight the need for therapies that target underlying pathogenic mechanisms rather than merely treating organ-specific symptoms. Phosphodiesterases, including phosphodiesterase 4B (PDE4B), are key regulators of cellular function and inflammatory responses of several cell types central to SSc pathogenesis. Given PDE4B's broad effects, targeting it may provide benefits beyond organ-specific manifestations and improve current care. Selective PDE4B inhibition represents a novel therapeutic approach for SSc, with improved subtype selectivity compared with earlier pan-PDE4 inhibitors. Nerandomilast preferentially inhibits PDE4B (ninefold over PDE4D), potentially improving tolerability versus oral pan-PDE4 inhibitors by avoiding adverse events such as gastrointestinal intolerance. Preclinical findings in SSc-relevant mouse and cell models show that PDE4B inhibition modulates inflammatory cytokine secretion, smooth muscle cell tension, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, and extracellular matrix synthesis under oxidative stress; this suggests nerandomilast could attenuate immune dysregulation, fibrosis, and potentially impact vasculopathy. Two pivotal Phase III trials evaluated nerandomilast in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (FIBRONEER™-IPF; NCT05321069) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (FIBRONEER™-ILD; NCT05321082), the latter of which included patients with SSc-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD). The ongoing CONQUEST trial (NCT06195072) is investigating the efficacy and safety of various drugs, including nerandomilast, in patients with early active SSc-ILD. This perspective highlights the rationale for targeting PDE4B in SSc therapy and explores preclinical findings in SSc and clinical findings in SSc-ILD to date.

items.title: Clinical variables and quantitative CT radiomics for mortality risk stratification after acute exacerbation of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy-associated interstitial lung disease.
items.abstract: Acute exacerbation (AE) is the most lethal event of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy-associated interstitial lung disease (IIM-ILD). This exploratory study compared clinical, radiomics, and combined predictor strategies across five survival-learning algorithms for survival risk stratification. We retrospectively analyzed 78 patients with AE-IIM-ILD and divided them into a training cohort (n = 54; 20 deaths) and a held-out internal testing cohort (n = 24; 9 deaths), stratified by observed mortality event status. Three predictor strategies were evaluated: a clinical strategy comprising PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio, neutrophil percentage (NEU%), and arthritis-related symptoms; a radiomics strategy comprising two selected radiomics features; and a combined strategy comprising PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio, arthritis-related symptoms, and a composite radiomics score (Rad-score). Each strategy was evaluated using five survival-learning algorithms. Harrell's concordance index (C-index) was the primary discrimination metric, with mean time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) used as a secondary measure. During the 1-year follow-up, 29 deaths were observed. Performance rankings varied across predictor strategies, algorithms, and evaluation metrics. The combined-Random Survival Forest configuration demonstrated the highest training-cohort C-index among the 15 configurations. Its mean time-dependent AUC was 0.923 (95% CI: 0.860-0.970) in the training cohort and 0.915 (95% CI: 0.736-0.986) in the testing cohort, with corresponding C-indices of 0.874 (95% CI: 0.803-0.940) and 0.842 (95% CI: 0.673-0.971), respectively. The model stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups with distinct observed survival trajectories. In this exploratory cohort, integrating selected clinical variables with a quantitative CT Rad-score using RSF showed promising numerical discrimination and risk-stratification performance. These findings suggest that clinical and quantitative imaging information may provide complementary prognostic information after AE-IIM-ILD.

items.title: Autoantibodies against interleukin-1 receptor antagonist in Still's disease in adult patients, data from a multicenter cohort study.
items.abstract: Emerging evidence supports the presence of autoantibodies targeting interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), a regulator of IL-1 signaling, in adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD). However, existing data are limited by small cohorts and potential confounding due to prior exposure to IL-1 inhibitors. This study aimed to develop a simple and reproducible indirect ELISA for detecting anti-IL-1Ra antibodies and to assess their frequency and immunological features in IL-1 inhibitor-naïve AOSD patients. Serum samples from IL-1 inhibitor-naïve AOSD patients (n=46) and healthy controls (n=26) were analyzed using an indirect ELISA based on recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) as antigen. Specificity was confirmed by dot blot. Anti-IL-1Ra IgG were affinity-purified from a high-titer patient and characterized by ELISA and SDS-PAGE. Epitope mapping was performed using phage display peptide libraries, followed by sequence alignment and structural mapping onto native IL-1Ra. Anti-IL-1Ra antibody levels were significantly higher in AOSD patients than in healthy controls (p=0.003), with a greater proportion showing high titers (p<0.001). Levels did not differ between active and inactive AOSD patients. Purified antibodies displayed specific dose-dependent binding to IL-1Ra. Phage display identified two peptide motifs corresponding to linear epitopes mapped to surface-exposed regions of the native protein, indicating recognition of unmodified IL-1Ra domains. Anti-IL-1Ra antibodies are detectable in IL-1 inhibitor-naïve AOSD patients using a standardized ELISA. The identification of distinct linear epitopes suggests a heterogeneous autoimmune response targeting IL-1Ra and may support a role for adaptive immunity within the Still's disease spectrum. Further studies are needed to define their functional and clinical relevance.

items.title: Associations of systemic inflammatory indices with rheumatoid arthritis and all-cause mortality: a NHANES study with independent hospital-based replication.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease associated with substantial morbidity and increased mortality. Although several composite inflammatory indices have been proposed as accessible biomarkers, their associations with RA and long-term prognosis remain incompletely understood. We analyzed 15,545 adults from five NHANES cycles (2001-2010), including 1,075 participants with self-reported RA. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was used to assess associations between inflammatory indices and prevalent RA. Among participants with RA, survey-weighted Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses were used to evaluate all-cause mortality. Restricted cubic spline analyses examined potential nonlinear associations. An independent retrospective hospital-based cohort was used to assess the directional consistency of key RA-related associations. Among 15,545 participants, 1,075 had self-reported RA. In the fully adjusted models, participants in the highest RAR quartile had greater odds of prevalent self-reported RA than those in the lowest quartile (OR, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.33-2.60), whereas higher CALLY was inversely associated with RA (Q4 vs. Q1: OR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.43-0.78); both associations remained significant after FDR correction. Among participants with self-reported RA, higher RAR was associated with a greater hazard of all-cause mortality (Q4 vs. Q1: HR, 2.48; 95% CI, 1.62-3.77), whereas higher CALLY was associated with a lower mortality hazard (Q4 vs. Q1: HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.31-0.61), with both associations remaining significant after FDR correction. Restricted cubic spline analyses suggested nonlinear associations for several inflammatory indices. In the independent hospital-based cohort, several key RA-related inflammatory indices showed directionally consistent associations, supporting the reproducibility of the principal RA-related findings. RAR and CALLY showed the most consistent associations with both prevalent RA and all-cause mortality. These accessible inflammatory indices may warrant further evaluation as markers of systemic inflammatory and nutritional status in RA, but prospective validation is needed before clinical application.

items.title: Translating the 2024 ACR lupus nephritis guidelines to pediatric practice.
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) is more common and often more aggressive in children than in adults, yet most randomized trials informing current LN management have enrolled adults. The 2024 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guideline is the first ACR guideline on lupus nephritis to explicitly state that its recommendations apply to both adults and children , although its evidence base remains largely adult-derived. This review uses the 2024 ACR guideline as an organizing framework, cross-referenced with the 2024 KDIGO and 2025 EULAR recommendations, to examine which aspects of LN management translate effectively to pediatric practice and which require caution. We review the diagnostic pathway, including screening, kidney biopsy, and ISN/RPS classification, as well as therapeutic strategies, including the shift from sequential dual therapy to upfront triple therapy, response targets, class-specific treatment, and selection between belimumab and calcineurin inhibitors. We then examine areas where pediatric evidence remains limited, particularly glucocorticoid dosing, long-term biologic safety, fertility and growth, and transition to adult care. While the fundamental principles of LN management are largely age-agnostic, many quantitative recommendations are not. Steroid dosing, long-term treatment exposure, and developmental consequences remain important pediatric-specific considerations that current guidelines cannot fully address. We conclude by highlighting the pediatric evidence available to date and the need for dedicated pediatric trials to replace adult-derived extrapolation with child-specific evidence.

items.title: Single-cell mass cytometry cartography highlights systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjögren's disease immune differences.
items.abstract: Autoimmune diseases such as primary Sjögren's disease (pSjD) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) share clinical and serological features, including type I interferon signatures, autoantibody formation, and chronic inflammation, but the underlying immunopathology is not the same. To support the development of targeted therapies, we aimed to systematically characterize disease-specific alterations in peripheral immune cell subsets of pSjD and SLE compared to healthy donors (HD). We analyzed peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 15 HD, 12 pSjD and 21 SLE patients by mass cytometry. We manually pre-gated viable CD19 + B cells, CD3 + T cells, and innate immune populations before performing high-dimensional, consensus clustering. We compared relative subset frequencies and marker expression, including costimulatory and inhibitory receptors, between the three cohorts. In the B cell compartment, we identified 13 clusters. SLE patients showed an relative expansion of plasmablasts and two double-negative (IgD - CD27 - ) B cell clusters, one CD21 - and one CD19 low with high IgA. Both had an activated phenotype with elevated CD38, CD86, and Ki-67. In SLE, the costimulatory molecules CD86 and CD226 were upregulated on memory and DN B cells. By contrast, B cell changes in pSjD were more modest. We found 12 T cells clusters. Both diseases had increased CD4 + PD-1 + ICOS + circulating T follicular helper-like cells, and pSjD showed expansion of CD8 + effector memory (Tem) and terminally differentiated (Temra) T cell subsets. Relative innate cell frequencies did not differ substantially between groups, however, intermediate CD226 hi monocytes were reduced in SLE but showed higher activation marker expression (CD86, HLA-DR). Network correlation analysis revealed higher immune-cell connectivity in SLE compared to pSjD. SLE is characterized by B cell activation, plasmablast expansion, and costimulatory upregulation, while pSjD is mainly defined by alterations in the CD8 + T cell compartment. These disease-specific immunologic signatures highlight distinct patterns in SLE and pSjD and generate hypotheses for future studies investigating targeted therapeutic approaches.

items.title: Identification of Akkermansia muciniphila as a candidate gut commensal involved in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: The "mucosal origins hypothesis" posits that mucosal sites, such as the gut, are initial sites where immune responses first develop that may, months to years later, result in clinical rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Our goal here was to conduct a discovery-based, hypothesis-generating study using samples from a relatively small number of patients to implicate previously unrecognized highly IgA-coated commensal flora that may have a role in RA pathogenesis (primary outcome). The secondary supporting outcomes were to determine whether HLA-DR-presented microbial peptides from such flora could be identified in synovial tissue and to determine T and B cell responses to these peptides and citrullinated proteins. Highly IgA-coated bacteria taxa were identified in RA patients' stool samples by 16s rRNA sequencing; HLA-DR-presented peptides derived from the most common, highly IgA-coated microbes were identified from synovial tissue by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry; T cell responses to the identified microbial and human mimic epitopes were determined by IFNγ ELISpot assays, and citrullinated IgG and IgA antibodies to implicated microbial and human proteins were measured by ELISA. Of 32 RA patients, 28 (88%) had highly IgA-coated Akkermansia muciniphila ( Am ) in stool samples. HLA-DR presentation of peptides derived from two Am proteins, including the molecular chaperone DnaK protein ( Am -cDnaK), was identified from RA synovial tissue, suggesting that the microbe or its components may reach the joints. Eight of 21 patients (38%) had T cell responses to the Am -cDnaK peptide and a human heat shock protein-mimic peptide (Hu-HSPA5) and/or IgG antibodies to citrullinated forms of these proteins. Reactivity was found primarily in pre-RA and early RA soon after transition to clinical RA and less commonly during later flares of arthritis. These data implicate Am as a candidate gut commensal involved in RA pathogenesis and may serve as a compass for planning larger studies to test the hypothesis that Am , as well as certain other highly IgA-coated commensal flora or their components, may sometimes reach joints where they initiate or enhance autoimmune T cell responses via epitope mimicry and epitope spreading, leading to antibody responses to citrullinated host proteins in joints.

items.title: Longitudinal monitoring of adalimumab levels and anti-adalimumab antibodies in Chinese patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a prospective cohort study.
items.abstract: This study aimed to clarify the association between longitudinal adalimumab concentrations, anti-adalimumab antibodies (AAA) levels, and clinical response in Chinese patients with ankylosing spondylitis (AS). A prospective multi-center, observational cohort study of AS patients receiving adalimumab therapy was conducted. Disease activity was assessed with the AS Disease Activity Score (ASDAS), and clinical responders were defined based on ASDAS improvement together with C-reactive protein normalization. Adalimumab concentrations were measured using a validated sandwich immunoassay. Measurement of AAA levels was performed with a laboratory-developed immunoassay system integrating electrochemiluminescence technology with specific immunomagnetic separation, with result reported as signal-to-noise ratio (S/N). A total of 140 patients receiving adalimumab monotherapy were included. The median follow-up period was 169 days, and 711 plasma samples were available for adalimumab concentrations and AAA levels measurements. Seven patients had pre-existing AAA, and 120 (90.2%) of the remaining 133 patients tested positive for AAA during follow-up. A total of 48 patients were excluded from the exposure-response relationship dataset owing to pre-existing AAA (n=7), lack of active disease (n=26), incomplete follow-up (n=8), and prolonged dosing intervals (n=7). Among the remaining 92 patients, a total of 58 (63%) achieved clinical response. Adalimumab concentrations were higher, and AAA levels were significantly lower, in responders compared with non-responders at multiple time points. Exposure-response relationship models also revealed a steady-state adalimumab concentration target of 5.1 μg/mL and a week-4 concentration target of 3.3 μg/mL, corresponding to an 80% probability of clinical response. Thirty-six of 92 patients (39.1%) exhibited AAA-S/N values exceeding the putative clinically meaningful threshold (AAA-S/N=10). Patients in the high-AAA group (AAA-S/N≥10) had lower drug levels (median: 1.5 μg/mL vs. 6.9 μg/mL, P< 0.0001) and poorer response rates (38.8% vs. 78.6%, P  = 0.0002), relative to those in the low-AAA group (AAA-S/N<10). Furthermore, patients who were week-4 AAA-positive exhibited a 1.8-fold increased risk of non-response (relative risk, 95% confidence interval, 1.1-2.8). Our results demonstrate that longitudinal profiles of adalimumab concentrations and AAA levels show a strong association with clinical responses in this Chinese AS cohort, which may inform therapeutic drug monitoring-guided adalimumab treatment strategies that remain to be further validated. items.title: Development of siRNAs targeting interferon beta as a novel therapeutic approach for adult and juvenile dermatomyositis.
items.abstract: A key feature of the autoimmune conditions adult and juvenile dermatomyositis (DM/JDM) is the correlation of interferon (IFN) beta induction with disease initiation and activity. Our aim was to establish a short interfering RNA (siRNA) approach to knockdown IFNB1 expression as a therapeutic strategy for DM/JDM. A library of 74 siRNAs targeting IFNB1 was designed and screened for IFNB1 knockdown by qRT-PCR. Lead siRNAs were analysed for secreted IFN beta protein reduction and acute cytotoxicity. IFNB1 expression was induced for efficacy screening in vitro , including in immortalised myoblasts, myotubes and dermal fibroblasts, alongside JDM patient-derived myotubes. RNA sequencing was also performed on siRNA treated and untreated dermal fibroblasts and patient myotubes. Initial screening of 27 siRNAs identified two lead siRNAs with significant knockdown of both IFN beta transcript and secreted protein in all cell lines, with one lead siRNA demonstrating a more favourable cytotoxicity profile. RNA sequencing and pathway analysis revealed that both lead siRNAs were able to reduce the induction of disease-associated immune and autoimmune pathways in dermal fibroblasts and JDM myotubes. An additional 47 siRNAs across the IFNB1 locus were screened; however, the previous lead siRNA remained the most active across relevant cell lines. Overall, comprehensive in vitro screening identified a lead siRNA targeting IFNB1 with significant mRNA and protein knockdown activity, low cytotoxicity and the ability to modulate immune-relevant pathways in muscle and skin cells. This is a promising first step towards the development of an siRNA therapy for DM/JDM and other conditions driven by IFN beta over-expression.

items.title: The neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus biomarker landscape: what blood and cerebrospinal fluid analytes have been studied and how they performed? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: This study aims to evaluate biomarkers that discriminate systemic lupus erythematosus patients with and without neuropsychiatric involvement. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL (inception-March 2024) for studies of blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analytes in neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE). Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for analyte-biofluid pairs with ≥5 independent studies; the remaining data were synthesized narratively. A total of 93 studies were included. Few analyte-biofluid combinations met the criteria for meta-analysis, and most promising biomarkers (intrathecal inflammation, neuronal injury, and reduced neuroprotection) were assessed in only small, heterogeneous studies. The meta-analyses showed higher CSF IL-6 and MCP-1 in NPSLE than non-NPSLE SLE (Hedges' g 0.81 and 0.66, respectively), a smaller heterogeneous effect for IL-8, and two- to threefold higher odds of NPSLE in patients positive for serum anti-ribosomal P (OR 2.68, 95% CI 2.03-3.53), anti-NR2/NMDAR (2.09, 1.07-4.06), and IgG anticardiolipin (2.36, 1.56-3.59) antibodies. Compared with non-SLE controls, NPSLE generally showed higher CSF soluble mediators than healthy or non-inflammatory neurological comparators, but the levels in CNS infections were often similar or higher. CSF markers of intrathecal inflammation, neuronal injury, and reduced neuroprotection distinguish NPSLE from non-NPSLE SLE but are neither specific for NPSLE nor easily obtainable in routine practice. Classical serum autoantibodies (anti-ribosomal P, anti-NR2, and antiphospholipid antibodies) show modest, phenotype-dependent diagnostic performance. Evidence remains fragmented, with heterogeneous assays, cutoffs, and case definitions, underscoring the need for harmonized multicenter studies to identify robust diagnostic, evaluative, and prognostic biomarkers for overall and manifestation-specific NPSLE.

items.title: Cross-sectional analysis of socioeconomic determinants of functional disability in rheumatoid arthritis patients: a single-region experience from Saudi Arabia.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients have increased disability risk, with physical inactivity and socioeconomic factors that are contributing to worse outcomes. Limited data exist on these relationships in Middle Eastern and Arab populations, and validated predictive models are scarce in the literature. Our study aims to assess physical activity levels and evaluate health-related quality of life and disability findings in RA patients from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and develop a sociodemographic risk-stratification model to quantify disability risk based on our cohort. We collected our data for the study from RA patients in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, through a disseminated cross-section survey for the eligible targeted cohort. Physical activity was assessed using IPAQ-S, disability using HAQ-DI, and sociodemographic characteristics through structured interviews. We developed a sociodemographic risk-stratification model using multiple linear regression with interaction terms, validated through 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap methods (1,000 iterations). Mediation analysis was performed to investigate education-employment-disability pathways. Risk stratification algorithms and utilization assessments were performed. Physical inactivity was highly prevalent, with the majority of included individuals reporting low physical activity levels. Mean HAQ-DI was 0.58 (SD 0.55). The model achieved a cross-validated R 2 of 0.188 (mean per-fold test R 2 = 0.122), reflecting the modest explanatory ceiling expected when only sociodemographic predictors are modeled, while still stratifying patients into low (58.2%), moderate (28.2%), and high (13.7%) disability risk categories. Education showed the strongest association with disability (ε 2 = 0.093, P < 0.0001), with employment partially mediating this relationship (13.4% mediation, 95% CI: 7.5-20.1%). Model calibration was significant, with utilization probability demonstrated across risk thresholds. We developed the first structured analysis for RA disability prediction in the region, revealing complete physical inactivity and significant socioeconomic disparities. Our analyses findings demonstrated evidence-based risk stratification for further consideration while identifying modifiable intervention targets. The results support population-level physical activity interventions and targeted socioeconomic support programs.

items.title: Engineering Tripterygium wilfordii -derived exosome-like nanoparticles for targeted therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Aim: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by excessive activation of pro-inflammatory macrophages and elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), resulting in synovial hyperplasia, cartilage destruction, and joint dysfunction. This study aimed to develop an engineered Tripterygium wilfordii -derived exosome-like nanoparticle system (TWELP@GlcN-HA) that integrates antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and joint-targeting activities for synergistic RA therapy. Methods: Tripterygium wilfordii -derived exosome-like nanoparticles (TWELP) were isolated from fresh Tripterygium wilfordii and sequentially surface-modified with glucosamine (GlcN) for cartilage protection and hyaluronic acid (HA) for targeted uptake by inflammatory cells. Their physicochemical properties, including morphology, particle size, structural integrity, and surface potential, were systematically characterized. In vitro assays were performed to evaluate ROS scavenging, inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokines [tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6)], and macrophage polarization. Biodistribution and therapeutic efficacy were evaluated in a collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse model by assessing synovial inflammation, cartilage damage, joint morphology, and joint function. Results: TWELP@GlcN-HA exhibited a uniform spherical morphology, stable surface potential, and preserved structural integrity. In vitro , it efficiently scavenged ROS, suppressed TNF-α and IL-6 secretion, and promoted macrophage polarization from M1 to M2, thereby restoring immune homeostasis. In vivo , HA-mediated targeting promoted nanoparticle accumulation in inflamed joints. TWELP@GlcN-HA significantly alleviated synovial inflammation and cartilage destruction, improved joint morphology and function, and exhibited excellent biosafety with no systemic toxicity. Conclusion: TWELP@GlcN-HA provides a multifunctional combinatorial strategy for RA treatment by synergistically regulating ROS, reprogramming pro-inflammatory macrophages, protecting cartilage, and achieving targeted joint delivery. Its enhanced therapeutic efficacy and favorable safety profile make it a promising candidate for future clinical translation in RA management.

items.title: The Bidirectional Relationship Between Rheumatoid Arthritis and Periodontitis: Current Evidence and Clinical Implications.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and periodontitis are chronic inflammatory diseases that share several pathogenic, immunological, and environmental characteristics. Increasing evidence suggests that these conditions are linked through a potentially bidirectional relationship in which chronic periodontal inflammation may contribute to the initiation and progression of RA, whereas RA may predispose individuals to periodontal tissue destruction through systemic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and impaired oral hygiene. This narrative review summarizes the current understanding of the epidemiological association between RA and periodontitis and discusses the shared inflammatory pathways, including cytokine dysregulation, osteoclast activation, and altered host immune responses, that underlie both diseases. Particular emphasis is placed on the reciprocal influence of periodontitis on RA activity and the impact of RA on periodontal disease. Available evidence indicates that periodontal infection may amplify the systemic inflammatory burden and autoimmune responses, whereas chronic inflammatory changes associated with RA can accelerate periodontal tissue breakdown and increase the risk of disease progression. Emerging clinical evidence also suggests that periodontal therapy may serve as a valuable adjunct to conventional RA management by reducing the systemic inflammatory burden and improving disease activity, although definitive causal relationships have not yet been established. Periodontal therapy may have beneficial effects on systemic inflammatory markers and selected measures of RA activity, although the clinical significance and consistency of these effects remain uncertain. Recognition of this bidirectional association highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between dental professionals and rheumatologists to facilitate early diagnosis, comprehensive patient assessment, and development of integrated treatment strategies. Future longitudinal and interventional studies are warranted to clarify the causal mechanisms linking these conditions and determine whether improved periodontal health can contribute to better long-term outcomes in patients with RA.

items.title: Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease in a Patient With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (KFD), or histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, is a rare, self-limiting syndrome characterized by fever and lymphadenopathy, most commonly cervical, though other nodal regions may be involved. It is well recognized to occur in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), with which it shares substantial clinical and histopathologic overlap, often mimicking a lupus flare or a lymphoproliferative disorder. We report the case of a 43-year-old woman with a known history of SLE, maintained on hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone, who presented with a two-week history of fever, chills, rigors, and generalized body aches. She was found to have elevated inflammatory markers, hypocomplementemia, a markedly elevated antinuclear antibody titer, and elevated anticardiolipin IgM, with imaging demonstrating marked right axillary and bilateral pelvic/iliac lymphadenopathy. Excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrated extensive necrotizing lymphadenitis with karyorrhectic debris and a predominantly T-cell infiltrate, without granulomas, and with negative infectious and Epstein-Barr virus studies, consistent with KFD. Bone marrow examination excluded an underlying hematologic malignancy, and a low HScore made hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis unlikely. The patient was treated with escalation of corticosteroid therapy and continuation of hydroxychloroquine, achieving clinical recovery with resolution of fever. This case highlights the importance of recognizing KFD as a cause of fever and lymphadenopathy in patients with SLE, and underscores the value of histopathologic confirmation in guiding appropriate management.

items.title: Gene expression signatures from single-cell transcriptomics predict Sjögren's syndrome.
items.abstract: Sjögren's syndrome (SjS) is a systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, leading to dry eyes and mouth. While previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and transcriptomic analyses have identified genes associated with SjS, predictive models based on single-cell resolution are limited. In this study, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of SjS patients were analyzed to map immune cell alterations linked to the disease. Compared with healthy controls, SjS patients displayed decreased proportions of naïve CD8 + T cells and Helios FOXP3 lo CD4 + Tregs, alongside increased frequencies of CTLA -4 + CD8 + inhibitory T cells and TRDC γδ T cells. Using machine learning, a predictive model for SjS diagnosis was developed based on a 12-gene signature (SjS. Sig: GIMAP7 , PSMB8 , CD27 , CCR7 , TAGAP , UQCR10 , HCLS1 , LCK , TNFAIP3 , ISG15 , GIMAP4 , and HLA - DRB1 ), which effectively differentiated patients from healthy individuals. Key genes such as CD27 , PSMB8 , HCLS1 , LCK , UQCR10 , and GIMAP4 were validated in clinical samples through flow cytometry and real-time quantitative PCR. These findings provide insights into the immune landscape of SjS at a single-cell resolution and propose a reliable molecular signature for diagnosis and immune monitoring.

items.title: Short-term risk and long-term incidence rate of herpes zoster with upadacitinib in patients with atopic dermatitis and psoriatic arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Upadacitinib is a novel selective Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitor. However, it increases the risk of herpes zoster infection. We aimed to estimate the short-term risk and long-term incidence rate of herpes zoster in patients with atopic dermatitis (AD) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) treated with different doses of upadacitinib. Randomised controlled trials and long-term (≥ 52 weeks) open-label extension studies of upadacitinib for AD and PsA were included. Short-term odds ratios (ORs) and long-term exposure-adjusted event rates (EAERs) for herpes zoster infection were estimated using R software 4.4.3 and STATA 18.0. This review included 8 randomised controlled studies and 11 open-label extension studies. The short-term analysis showed that in AD patients, the ORs for herpes zoster infection after 15 mg and 30 mg upadacitinib were 2.62 (95% CI: 1.06-6.47) and 3.13 (95% CI: 1.38-7.12), respectively. In PsA patients, the ORs were 1.39 (95% CI: 0.45-4.33) and 2.43 (95% CI: 0.96-6.16), respectively. The long-term analysis showed that the EAER for herpes zoster infection in AD and PsA patients using 15 mg upadacitinib was 1 year: 3.87/100 patient-years (PYs), 2 years: 4.68/100 PYs, and 3 years: 4.30/100 PYs; for 30 mg, the EAER was 1 year: 6.96/100 PYs, 2 years: 8.29/100 PYs, and 3 years: 7.53/100 PYs. Upadacitinib 30 mg was associated with a significantly higher risk of herpes zoster compared with 15 mg, with consistent dose-dependent effects at 1-year (OR = 1.78, 95% CI: 1.41-2.24), 2-year (OR = 1.80, 95% CI: 1.28-2.53), and 3-year follow-up (OR = 1.94, 95% CI: 1.59-2.35). Upadacitinib increases the risk of herpes zoster in AD and PsA patients, with a more significant effect in AD patients and a dose-dependent relationship over time.

items.title: Divergent approaches to rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease: a comparative analysis of international clinical practice guidelines.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. We compared international and regional clinical practice guidelines to identify agreement, differences, and gaps in RA-ILD care. We conducted a narrative comparative review of five guideline groups: ERS/EULAR, ACR/CHEST, EULAR, PANLAR, and ALAT. Recommendations were assessed across screening, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment, together with their methodological approaches. Diagnostic recommendations showed the greatest agreement: ILD-focused guidelines emphasized high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), pulmonary function tests, and multidisciplinary evaluation. Screening recommendations differed: ERS/EULAR and ACR/CHEST favored risk-based assessment, whereas ALAT proposed a broader approach that included lung ultrasound as an adjunct, without replacing HRCT. For established RA-ILD, ACR/CHEST suggested, as implementation guidance, pulmonary function testing every 3-12 months during the first year and HRCT when clinically indicated; ERS/EULAR proposed pulmonary function testing every 3-6 months in the first years and periodic HRCT. Treatment showed the greatest divergence. ACR/CHEST conditionally recommended mycophenolate, rituximab, azathioprine, and cyclophosphamide as first-line ILD therapies, whereas ALAT emphasized integrated control of articular and pulmonary disease, particularly with abatacept or rituximab. EULAR and PANLAR primarily addressed RA treatment and did not provide dedicated RA-ILD algorithms. Antifibrotic treatment was considered mainly in progressive fibrosing disease. Guidelines converge on HRCT-based evaluation but differ in screening, monitoring intervals, and treatment priorities. These differences reflect their scope, methodology, and limited RA-ILD-specific evidence. Prospective comparative studies are needed to inform more consistent care.

items.title: Changes in biventricular myocardial function after six months of ixekizumab therapy in patients with psoriatic arthritis: a prospective speckle-tracking echocardiographic study.
items.abstract: To evaluate longitudinal changes in conventional and speckle-tracking echocardiographic indices in patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA) who achieved a disease activity index for psoriatic arthritis (DAPSA)-defined clinical response during ixekizumab therapy.In this prospective single-centre observational cohort, 21 adults with PsA underwent clinical, laboratory and transthoracic echocardiographic assessment before ixekizumab initiation and after 6 months of treatment. The principal echocardiographic outcome was the within-patient change in absolute left vetricle global longitudinal strain (LV GLS) between baseline and 6 months. Secondary echocardiographic outcomes included right ventricle (RV) GLS, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), tricuspid annular systolic velocity (RV S') and tricuspid E to E' ratio (E/E'), while clinical secondary outcomes included DAPSA, body surface area (BSA), minimal disease activity (MDA), C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Mean age was 49.6 ± 11.6 years, 57.1% were male and 11 patients (52.4%) were biologic-naïve. MDA was achieved by 17 patients (81.0%). DAPSA decreased from 28.9 ± 4.3 to 7.7 ± 4.2, accompanied by reductions in CRP and ESR (all p < 0.001). Absolute LV GLS increased from 18.5 ± 1.3% to 20.5 ± 1.9% (mean change 2.0%, 95% CI 1.49-2.51; p < 0.001), while absolute RV GLS increased from 21.5 ± 3.3% to 25.8 ± 4.2% (mean change 4.29%, 95% CI 3.37-5.20; p < 0.001). LVEF, TAPSE, RV S' and E/E' also improved significantly. Although DAPSA reduction correlated with increased LVEF, while BSA reduction with increased LV GLS and TAPSE, these associations were exploratory and should be interpreted cautiously. Among patients with PsA who achieved clinical response to ixekizumab, 6 months of treatment was accompanied by improvements in left- and right-ventricular functional indices. Because the cohort was small, responder-enriched and lacked a comparator group, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger controlled studies.

items.title: Tocilizumab for active rheumatoid arthritis in a patient with concomitant primary biliary cholangitis: a case based review.
items.abstract: The coexistence of active rheumatoid arthritis and active primary biliary cholangitis represents a distinct therapeutic challenge. Evidence-based guidance for treatment selection in this clinical setting remains limited, and published experience with tocilizumab is restricted to isolated case reports. We report a 59-year-old woman with highly active, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and marked cholestatic biochemical activity, in whom diagnostic evaluation revealed active primary biliary cholangitis in the absence of advanced liver fibrosis. Following multidisciplinary assessment, methotrexate and leflunomide were avoided because of active cholestatic liver disease, and treatment with subcutaneous tocilizumab was initiated in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid and fenofibrate. Tocilizumab was well tolerated and led to a progressive improvement in arthritis. In parallel, cholestatic liver parameters showed sustained improvement in the absence of hepatic adverse effects. To contextualize this observation, we performed a focused literature review and identified only two directly relevant case reports, both reporting favorable rheumatologic and hepatic outcomes during tocilizumab therapy. This case adds to the limited body of evidence suggesting that tocilizumab may represent a feasible therapeutic option for selected patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and concomitant primary biliary cholangitis.

items.title: Impact of the Sociodemographic Index on Efficacy/Safety of Tofacitinib in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: Post Hoc Analysis of Phase 2/3/3b/4 Studies.
items.abstract: We explored the impact of the Sociodemographic Index (SDI) on the efficacy/safety of tofacitinib and adalimumab in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). This post hoc analysis used data from phase 2/3/3b/4 studies of patients with RA receiving tofacitinib 5 or 10 mg twice daily (BID), adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks, or placebo. Patients were stratified into country-level SDI tertiles (low/medium/high; defined as Global Burden of Disease 2010 scores of ≤ 0.708/> 0.708-≤ 0.803/> 0.803). Efficacy/patient-reported outcomes were evaluated to month (M)3. We calculated incidence rates (IRs) for safety outcomes through M24. Pooled data are reported for tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg BID. Patients: low SDI, N = 1969; medium SDI, N = 1538; high SDI, N = 3071. There was a higher percentage of patients aged ≥ 50 years, ever smokers, and prior biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug users, and RA duration was longer, in the high vs low/medium SDI tertiles. Across SDI tertiles, efficacy at M3 was generally greater with tofacitinib or adalimumab vs placebo. Odds ratios vs placebo showed that American College of Rheumatology 20/70 responses at M3 for tofacitinib or adalimumab were numerically greatest (i.e., 95% confidence intervals [CIs] overlapped) in the high SDI tertile. Placebo-adjusted least squares mean change from baseline in Disease Activity Score in 28 joints with C-reactive protein/erythrocyte sedimentation rate and Clinical Disease Activity Index at M3 was greater in the high vs low/medium SDI tertile (95% CIs overlapped) with tofacitinib or adalimumab. For tofacitinib or adalimumab, IRs for adverse events/serious adverse events were numerically greatest in the high SDI tertile. Efficacy at M3 was at least numerically greater with tofacitinib or adalimumab vs placebo, regardless of SDI. Placebo-adjusted efficacy responses were at least numerically greater in patients from high SDI countries. Safety IRs were also generally numerically greatest in the high SDI tertile with tofacitinib or adalimumab. Results were confounded by differences in demographics/baseline characteristics and associated lifestyle factors between SDI tertiles. items.title: The ASAS core set for the assessment of axial spondyloarthritis in clinical practice.
items.abstract: To develop the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) core set for the assessment of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) in clinical practice. This entails defining an internationally endorsed and clinically feasible guiding set of domains and corresponding instruments that considers both the assessment scenarios of 'routine' and 'extended' outpatient visits. A scoping literature review and Delphi survey among stakeholders (ASAS members, non-ASAS member rheumatologists, and patients) informed the selection of clinically relevant domains and instruments for the core set. The selected domains and instruments were presented and discussed with the ASAS community at the 2026 ASAS annual meeting, and voted upon for endorsement. Following discussion with the ASAS community, the core set was endorsed by a majority of ASAS members. Five domains are included for routine visits: 'disease activity', 'pain', 'peripheral manifestations', 'extra-musculoskeletal manifestations', and 'treatment aspects', with 1 instrument recommended for each domain, alongside several optional instruments. Four supplementary domains are included for extended visits (to be assessed in addition to all routine visit domains): 'structural damage', 'overall functioning and health', 'comorbidities', and 'mobility', with at least 1 recommended or optional instrument incorporated for each domain. The ASAS core set for the assessment of axSpA in clinical practice represents the minimum domains to be systematically assessed in all patients during routine and extended visits, with corresponding instruments. Its development marks a step towards improved standardisation of disease assessments in axSpA in the clinical setting, providing a practical framework that aligns with existing management recommendations.

items.title: Associations between methodological quality and representation in clinical trials of systemic lupus erythematosus therapies.
items.abstract: BackgroundRandomized clinical trials support drug development and uptake of new therapies for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, challenges to conducting high-quality clinical trials have been noted, including underrepresentation of minoritized populations. Currently, it is not known whether the methodological quality of clinical trials is associated with representativeness of US patients with SLE.MethodsFor this cross-sectional study, we identified industry-sponsored clinical trials of small molecules and biologics for SLE with at least one US enrollment site, with results published in peer-reviewed journals as of January 1, 2026. Trial characteristics were abstracted, and urbanicity of US enrollment sites were classified using the National Center for Health Statistics Urban-Rural Classification System. Trial representativeness by sex, race, and ethnicity were assessed against SLE prevalence in meta-analyzed US lupus registries using participation-to-prevalence ratios (PPRs; ≥0.8 indicating adequate representation). Trial methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Associations between trial risk of bias and representativeness were evaluated.FindingsWe identified 51 trials enrolling 18,466 participants with SLE. Trial representation was adequate for female (median PPR 1 · 03), Hispanic (median PPR 1 · 37), White (median PPR 1 · 03), and Asian participants (median PPR 2 · 40), and Black participants were underrepresented (median PPR 0 · 32). Most US enrollment sites were located in large metropolitan areas. The methodological quality of trials varied (37% at low risk of bias, 35% with some concerns, 27% at high risk of bias) but was not associated with demographic or geographic representativeness.InterpretationWe identified inconsistencies in participant representation and methodological quality across SLE clinical trials. Although trial designs were generally rigorous, limitations of participant inclusion and enrollment site distribution suggest that representation, rather than methodological quality alone, may limit the external validity of SLE clinical trials.

items.title: Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6-dependent manner.
items.abstract: Psychological stress affects the immune system and exacerbates autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the mechanisms underlying tissue inflammation during remission remain unclear. Here, we show that tube restraint stress exacerbates joint inflammation in a murine arthritis model during remission. This exacerbation required interleukin-6 (IL-6) produced by brown adipose tissue (BAT) following sympathetic activation. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes expressing the IL-6 receptor subunit gp130 were critical mediators, as IL-6 stimulated these cells to produce the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1. Pharmacological blockade of the β3-adrenergic receptor significantly attenuated stress-induced arthritis flares. In patients with RA, carriers of the hypofunctional Trp64Arg variant of ADRB3 showed no positive correlation between psychological stress and disease activity, whereas noncarriers did. These findings identify a BAT-IL-6-fibroblast axis that reactivates inflammatory memory in arthritis and suggest that targeting stress-responsive pathways may provide a complementary therapeutic strategy alongside current RA treatments without broadly suppressing systemic immunity.

items.title: Identifying diagnostic testing gaps for antiphospholipid syndrome within a single healthcare system.
items.abstract: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) is a rare disease with significant morbidity and the possibility of mortality. While there are no established diagnostic criteria for use in clinical settings, there is a large body of global research organized by the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (ACR/EULAR) into accepted research guidelines, developed for identifying probable APS cases. The research guidelines were used in this study as a surrogate approach for evaluating diagnostic testing patterns, with the aim of identifying potential gaps in patient evaluation for APS in clinical settings. For this study, suggested testing for APS characterization included IgG (Immunoglobulin G) and IgM (Immunoglobulin M) anti-cardiolipin antibodies; IgG and IgM anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies; and Lupus Anticoagulant. This retrospective cross-sectional study identified patients from the electronic medical records of a regional health system with International Classification of Diseases (ICD) diagnostic codes for APS-associated conditions, signs, symptoms, and/or testing collected for antiphospholipid antibodies in selected medical and surgical specialty locations, from 01/01/2011 to 12/31/2020. These data were used to assess how closely the clinical testing patterns followed the 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria for laboratory evaluation. The data showed that 80.70% of 16679 patients with antiphospholipid antibody tests collected did not include all antiphospholipid antibody testing described in 2023 ACR/EULAR research criteria guidelines. These findings may represent common suboptimal ordering practices in evaluations for APS, highlighting the need for peer comparison and the development of future clinical laboratory guidance to support more complete assessment for APS.

items.title: Cytokine-involved phenotyping identifies a high-risk inflammatory cluster in treatment-naïve Takayasu's arteritis.
items.abstract: Takayasu's arteritis (TAK) is a clinically heterogeneous large-vessel vasculitis. Conventional inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) may not adequately reflect underlying immune activation or predict long-term outcomes. We aimed to identify immune phenotypes based on serum cytokine profiles and evaluate their clinical relevance in treatment-naïve TAK. We performed an unsupervised two-step cluster analysis in a cohort of 95 treatment-naïve patients with TAK. Serum levels of 12 cytokines were measured at baseline and clustering incorporated cytokine profiles together with selected clinical variables, including age at onset, disease duration, ESR and CRP. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using multivariable Cox regression models adjusting for disease duration and treatment exposure. A cytokine-involved scoring system was developed for phenotype classification and internally evaluated. Three distinct immune phenotypes were identified. Cluster 2 exhibited multiplex cytokine activation, characterised by elevated interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-10, tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interferon (IFN)-α with the worst outcomes: high relapse (50.0%), refractory disease (41.7%), and mortality (16.7%). Cluster 1 showed an acute phase response (high ESR, CRP, IL-6, IFN-γ), more active disease, and increased relapse risk (41.7%). Cluster 3 had a noninflammatory phenotype, the highest remission (74.5%), and lowest relapse (4.3%). A cytokine-involved scoring model accurately classified phenotype (accuracy 85.2%, AUC 0.964). Cytokine-involved phenotyping may provide a preliminary framework for risk stratification in treatment-naïve TAK. The multiplex cytokine activation phenotype appears to be associated with adverse clinical outcomes, although further validation in larger cohorts is required.

items.title: Damage accrual predicts the development of lymphoma in primary Sjögren's disease.
items.abstract: To study whether damage and its kinetics are associated with mortality and lymphoma development in primary Sjögren's disease (pSjD). Single-centre retrospective cohort study including patients with pSjD. Damage was assessed yearly using the Sjögren Syndrome (SS) damage index (DI) (SSDI) and SS Disease DI (SSDDI) scores. Early damage: damage occurring in the first year after diagnosis; early damage increase: increase of ≥1 point in the first 5 years. SSDDI and SSDI scores' domains were compared with two-sample test of proportions. Cox regression was performed to investigate predictors of mortality and lymphoma. A p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. We included 208 patients with pSjD (female: 93.8%; mean age at diagnosis/onset: 49.9±14.9/45.6±15.0 years; mean follow-up time: 14.1±9.2 years). Damage affected 79.3% and 85.1% patients, using SSDDI and SSDI scores, respectively. Age at diagnosis (per one-unit increase HR 1.1, 95%CI 1.1-1.2) and at onset (per one-unit increase HR 1.1, 95%CI 1.0-1.2) predicted mortality. Damage and early damage increase did not predict mortality with either score. Seventeen patients (8.2%) developed lymphoma. Early damage increases predicted lymphoma in both scores (SSDDI: HR 14.5, 95% CI 1.8-115; SSDI: HR 12.8, 95% CI 1.5-108.1). Early damage variation, damage variation, and cumulative damage were also predictors of lymphoma. Although damage was not associated with mortality, age at diagnosis and onset of symptoms were risk factors for mortality in pSjD. Cumulative and evolving damage, especially in the first years of disease, should raise concern about the possible development of lymphoma in these patients.

items.title: Clinical performance of obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome classification criteria: an ambispective cohort study.
items.abstract: To evaluate the clinical performance of the 2006 Sydney and 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome (OAPS), compare subsequent pregnancy outcomes across classifications and develop a supplementary classification method to further identify clinically relevant non-criteria OAPS (NC-OAPS) cases missed by the Sydney-derived NC-OAPS classification. This single-center ambispective cohort included 1741 women of reproductive age enrolled from January 2020 to October 2024. Expert consensus was used to classify participants into OAPS, NC-OAPS and non-OAPS groups. The clinical performance of the 2006 Sydney criteria, 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria and Sydney-derived NC-OAPS classification were assessed. The subsequent pregnancy outcomes were followed up and compared across different groups. Moreover, a supplementary NC-OAPS classification method was developed and validated. The Sydney criteria identified expert-defined OAPS with sensitivity 0.806, specificity 0.991 and AUC 0.898. The 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria showed lower sensitivity (0.267) but near-perfect specificity (0.999). Live birth rates were similar among expert-defined OAPS, NC-OAPS and non-OAPS after treatment, but OAPS had higher rates of preterm birth, fetal growth restriction and severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. Patients fulfilling 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria had poorer pregnancy outcomes than those identified by expert consensus or the Sydney criteria. In the validation folds, the supplementary method yielded a sensitivity of 0.732 and a specificity of 0.921. The 2006 Sydney criteria remain more suitable for clinical identification of OAPS, whereas the 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria may be useful for high-risk stratification. The supplementary classification method may improve recognition of NC-OAPS patients missed by existing criteria.

items.title: The long-term impact of juvenile idiopathic arthritis into adulthood: a systematic review.
items.abstract: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), a childhood-onset chronic condition, often persists into adulthood. However, most studies investigating outcomes of JIA are limited to childhood, missing the long-term impact of the condition. This systematic literature review aimed to: identify the frequency of children with JIA that (i) continue to have active disease in adulthood, (ii) have limited functional ability in adulthood, (iii) are impacted by mental health problems in adulthood, and (iv) describe the impact of JIA on quality of life in adulthood compared with non-JIA peers. The literature was searched for published reports of observational studies that measured outcomes in adults aged 18 years or over with an existing diagnosis of JIA. Outcomes of interest included disease activity, functional ability, mental health, and quality of life. Forty-four studies were included. When limited to studies that identified participants during childhood, 33-66% of adults with JIA had active disease, and 28-58% had limited functional ability. Mental health diagnoses were found in up to 19% of adults with JIA, and physical health-related quality of life measures were consistently lower in adults with JIA compared with non-JIA comparators. Despite being a childhood-onset condition, a substantial proportion of adults with JIA experience active disease, limited functional ability, and mental health problems beyond 18 years old, as well as report poorer physical health-related quality of life. This is valuable information to support future research into the impact of JIA in adulthood, and how best to support individuals throughout the life-course of their condition.

items.title: The trajectory of gout: mapping pathogenic cell states from flares to tophus.
items.abstract: The clinical course of gout is typically divided into four stages: asymptomatic hyperuricemia, gout flares, intercritical gout and tophaceous gout. However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving transitions between these stages remain unclear. Current clinical practice lacks stage-specific precision therapeutic strategies. In recent years, the development of single-cell sequencing technologies has provided tools to reveal dynamic cell state transitions during gout progression. This review synthesizes existing single-cell evidence to systematically delineate the immune and stromal cell landscapes across the stages of gout, and explores their roles in inflammation initiation, spontaneous resolution, and tissue remodeling, with the aim to provide a theoretical framework for stage-adapted therapies.

items.title: Outcomes of systemic sclerosis with overlapping myositis: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) carries the highest disease-specific mortality among rheumatic diseases, with cardiac involvement and interstitial lung disease (ILD) as leading causes of death. We aimed to determine whether overlapping myositis independently contributes to cardiac involvement and mortality in SSc. We did a 1:1 propensity score matched retrospective cohort study of 880 SSc patients (2013 ACR/EULAR criteria) at a single centre. SSc myositis required proximal weakness and elevated muscle enzymes without alternative causes. Cardiac involvement used SCTC criteria (pericardial effusion, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmia, conduction disease). We used standard and Firth penalised logistic regression for cardiac predictors, Cox regression for survival, and Fisher's exact test for cause specific mortality. All p values were Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted. Of 880 patients, 92 (10.4%) had myositis. After matching, 92 pairs (n = 184) were analysed. Myositis independently predicted cardiac involvement (standard aOR=19.99, 95%CI 2.19-182.26, p = 0.008; Firth OR = 12.84, 95%CI 2.31-98.47, p = 0.006). Higher mRSS also predicted cardiac involvement (aOR=2.34 per 10 points, p = 0.006). Anti-Scl70 was less common in myositis (25.0% vs. 50.0%, p = 0.009). Overall mortality did not differ (13.0% vs. 9.8%, p = 0.620). In non-myositis deaths, ILD caused 33.3%; in myositis deaths, cardiac failure caused 25% and no ILD-related deaths (Fisher's p = 0.229). Cardiac involvement was significantly associated with mortality (aHR=8.09 (1.36-48.26), p = 0.022), independent of myositis. Overlapping myositis in SSc is associated with an increased risk of cardiac involvement and a shift in the cause-of-death profile away from ILD, without a detectable difference in overall survival over the observed median 21-month follow-up. Systematic cardiac surveillance is needed in these patients.

items.title: Perioperative B-Cell-Targeted Therapy for High-Risk Valve Surgery in Active Primary Sjögren's Disease.
items.abstract: Primary Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by B-cell dysregulation. Clinically significant valvular involvement is uncommon, and evidence guiding perioperative immunomodulation remains limited. A 59-year-old woman with SjD and severe aortic stenosis required valve replacement. Preoperative evaluation demonstrated active SjD with elevated inflammatory markers and hypergammaglobulinemia. Following multidisciplinary discussion, telitacicept, corticosteroids, and hydroxychloroquine were initiated before surgery. After improvement in inflammatory activity, the patient underwent aortic valve and ascending aorta replacement. Histopathologic examination showed degenerative valvular changes with focal inflammatory cell infiltration. The postoperative course was uneventful, with normal prosthetic valve function at 1-year follow-up. This case highlights the challenges of managing severe valvular heart disease in patients with active primary SjD and a multidisciplinary perioperative strategy incorporating B-cell-targeted therapy. Although preoperative immunomodulation may have attenuated the histopathologic evidence of immune-mediated valvular involvement, the case offers insights when guidance is limited.

items.title: Gout May Mimic Infection, Even Years After Achilles Tendon Repair.
items.abstract: Gout can affect tendons in addition to joints and may clinically resemble infection. The resulting diagnostic uncertainty may lead to surgical intervention or antibiotic treatment, even in patients whose symptoms might be managed medically if gout is recognized earlier. (1) Does late-onset gouty Achilles tendinopathy after prior Achilles tendon repair clinically resemble infection? (2) What diagnostic findings, including crystal analysis of aspirate or surgically obtained material when available, helped establish or support gout rather than infection? (3) What were the outcomes after gout was confirmed or suspected? This is a report of 4 patients with a similar presentation. Between April 2021 and June 2024, three surgeons at three academic medical centers identified 4 adult males, aged 42 to 55 years, who developed acute atraumatic Achilles-region pain, swelling, erythema, drainage, fluctuance, or induration 2 to 18 years after open Achilles tendon repair. These presentations raised concern that gout at or near a prior Achilles tendon repair site may mimic infection and lead to unnecessary interventions when gout is not considered early. We do not have an underlying denominator of patients treated for Achilles tendon repair by these surgeons during this period, but we speculate that it is on the order of several hundred. Minimum follow-up was 6 months after the treatment selected for the index Achilles inflammatory presentation. No patients who met these criteria were excluded, and no patients were lost to follow-up before the minimum follow-up interval. To determine whether this presentation clinically resembled infection, we reviewed presenting symptoms and physical examination findings, including pain, swelling, erythema, drainage, fluctuance, induration, fever, constitutional symptoms, and the treating surgeon's initial diagnostic concern. To answer our second question regarding diagnostic findings that established or supported gout rather than infection, we reviewed laboratory studies, imaging, aspiration findings, Gram stain, bacterial cultures, surgical findings, and pathologic evaluation for monosodium urate crystals. To answer our third question regarding outcomes, we reviewed whether patients underwent aspiration, surgical irrigation and debridement, antibiotics, immobilization, antiinflammatory or urate-lowering therapy, rheumatology or infectious disease referral, symptom resolution, recurrence, and complications. Three patients underwent aspiration and/or surgical irrigation and debridement for presumed infection. One patient was treated nonsurgically for suspected gout. In 3 of 4 patients, late-onset gouty Achilles tendinopathy after prior Achilles tendon repair clinically resembled infection; it raised concern for an acute inflammatory or infectious process in all 4 patients. Among the 3 patients treated surgically, chalky tophaceous material was identified adjacent to the Achilles tendon, bacterial cultures were negative, and histological analysis confirmed monosodium urate crystals. The fourth patient had suspected gout based on hyperuricemia, Achilles-region symptoms, and improvement with nonsurgical treatment, although gout was not pathologically confirmed. All patients reported symptom resolution by latest follow-up (6 to 16 months). Acute gouty tendinopathy can present years after Achilles tendon repair and can closely mimic postoperative infection, even when serum uric acid is normal. In patients without systemic signs of sepsis, earlier consideration of gout and routine crystal analysis when aspirate or surgically obtained material is available may help avoid unnecessary surgical debridement or prolonged empiric antibiotics when infection is not otherwise supported. Level IV, therapeutic study.

items.title: Integrated Multiomics Profiling Reveals Membrane-Associated Signaling Alterations Associated With Disease Activity in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by pervasive immune dysregulation, yet membrane-associated molecular alterations in immune cells remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a self-established cohort of 130 SLE patients across disease stages and 90 healthy controls, with individual samples pooled into 36 samples for LC-MS/MS analysis, complemented by publicly available transcriptomic data from 1461 SLE patients. Focusing on membrane-associated proteins, we identified alterations in protein abundance and phosphorylation involving cytoskeletal organization, cell adhesion, and membrane trafficking, with the RHO GTPase cycle consistently enriched in both omic layers. Dynamic multisite phosphorylation of FLNA and increased abundance of FLNB and FNBP1 were observed. Clustering revealed distinct disease-stage-associated patterns involving integrin proteins in SLE in remission (SLE_R) and cytoskeletal and mechanotransduction components in active SLE (SLE_A). OAS3 and IFIT5 showed concordant transcript-protein changes, while interferon- and NF-κB-related transcriptional programs were implicated. Computational kinase analysis identified disease-stage-associated predicted activity patterns involving PKC, MAPKs, CDKs, and CaM-Ks. Together, these findings provide a multiomics view of membrane-associated molecular alterations associated with disease activity in SLE.

items.title: IgG4-Related Disease Presenting as Inflammatory Midline Pseudotumor of the Face and Neck.
items.abstract: A 78-year-old Chinese woman presented with a one-year history of a progressively enlarging purpuric rash over the central face and nasal dorsum, with subsequent development of a firm midline neck mass. She responded well to prednisolone. This case illustrates a rare cutaneous presentation of IgG4-RD, which should be considered in differential diagnoses of head and neck lesions.

items.title: Association between serum transaminase elevations and clinical course in patients with familial Mediterranean fever.
items.abstract: To evaluate the clinical features, disease course, genetics, and treatment responses of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) patients with elevated serum transaminase levels. The charts of the FMF patients with at least one year of follow-up were retrospectively investigated for the presence of elevated serum transaminase levels. The genetic and clinical findings and disease course of identified patients were compared with a group of FMF patients with no transaminase elevations. A retrospective chart review included 780 registered patients diagnosed with FMF. Forty-two patients (5.3%) were excluded because of the insufficient follow-up duration, associated viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, and biopsy-proven liver amyloidosis. A total of 83 patients (11.2%) with elevated serum transaminase levels were identified, and their findings were compared with a control group of 655 patients with no transaminase elevation. FMF attacks began at a significantly older age (17.0±12.9 vs. 12.4±9.0 years, p=0.01), and the percentage of patients experiencing more frequent (≥ 3 attacks/month) attacks was higher (35.4% vs. 24.1%, p=0.01) in the elevated transaminase group. No significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding age at diagnosis, delay in diagnosis, presenting features of FMF, CRP levels at baseline and during attacks, frequency of amyloidosis, and the colchicine dose, as well as the frequency of patients requiring anti-IL-1 treatments. The frequency of MEFV gene exon 10 mutations and p.M694V homozygosity did not differ significantly between the groups. Hepatosteatosis was observed by abdominal ultrasonography in 46.7% of the patients with elevated liver enzymes. A follow-up study after 6 years revealed that transaminase levels remained elevated in 21 out of 49 patients (42.9%), and one patient developed liver cirrhosis. Elevated serum transaminase levels can be detected in approximately 11.2% of FMF patients, and this finding is not associated with colchicine use or manifestations of FMF. Ultrasonographic evidence of hepatosteatosis was observed in nearly half of the patients. Follow-up analysis showed that serum transaminase elevations may persist in 43% of the patients, which suggests further studies to determine whether this abnormality is a feature of FMF or not.

items.title: Clinical Factors Associated with Diagnostic Delay in Axial Spondyloarthritis in Saudi Arabia: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : Diagnostic delay remains a major challenge in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), yet factors associated with delay in Saudi Arabia and the Arabian Gulf remain poorly characterized. We examined clinical factors associated with diagnostic delay in a single-center Saudi cohort. Methods : This retrospective cohort included 160 of 220 screened registry patients with rheumatologist-confirmed axSpA who fulfilled ASAS classification criteria. Diagnostic delay was measured in whole years from documented symptom onset to diagnosis. Twenty-four patients had fibromyalgia documented before axSpA diagnosis. The primary negative binomial model included sex, axSpA subtype, HLA-B27 status, documented prediagnosis fibromyalgia, and symptom-onset age; logistic regression evaluated delay > 5 years. Standardized predictions estimated absolute differences, and a 2-year landmark analysis reduced differential opportunity for fibromyalgia ascertainment. Results : Median delay was 3 years (IQR 2-6), and 41 patients (25.6%) had delay >5 years. Documented prediagnosis fibromyalgia was associated with longer expected delay (ratio of expected diagnostic delays, 1.59; 95% CI 1.24-2.04; p < 0.001), corresponding to an adjusted difference of 2.33 years (bootstrap 95% CI 0.87-4.13), and with greater odds of delay >5 years (OR 5.56; 95% CI 2.08-14.85). Older symptom-onset age was also associated with longer delay. In the landmark analysis ( n = 107), fibromyalgia documented by 2 years remained associated with longer subsequent delay (ratio of expected diagnostic delays, 1.51; 95% CI 1.05-2.19; p = 0.027). Conclusions : Documented prediagnosis fibromyalgia and older symptom-onset age were associated with longer diagnostic delay. The fixed-window landmark analysis reduced concern about differential ascertainment opportunity but remained subject to selection and reverse causation and did not establish causality. Persistent features suggestive of inflammatory axial disease in patients with fibromyalgia warrant selective diagnostic reconsideration.
